conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi, I'm Dr. Lee. I understand you've been having severe abdominal pain. Can you tell me more about it?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yeah, it started about ten days ago. It’s sharp, like a knife, and it goes from my upper belly down to my lower back.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: And does eating make it worse?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, every time I eat, it gets worse. I’ve been vomiting a lot—couldn’t keep anything down.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I see. You mentioned you had one episode of vomiting blood?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Just once. That’s when they sent me to the ER before, but I was sent home. The pain never got better.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: And today, in the clinic, they gave you fentanyl for pain and you developed a rash?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yeah, it was itchy all over. Then they sent me here.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We gave you Benadryl for the rash, and Dilaudid for pain. You also had some eye fluttering in triage—did you lose consciousness?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: No, I was awake the whole time. It felt weird, but I didn’t pass out or bite my tongue.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Okay, that’s reassuring. We’ll monitor that. For now, your labs are mostly stable. Your lipase is normal, which is unusual for pancreatitis flare, but given your history, we think this is chronic pancreatitis with worsening pain.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So it’s not an infection or something new?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: No signs of infection. Your white count is slightly up, but not concerning. We did a KUB—no blockage or free air. We’re going to do an MRCP tomorrow to get a detailed look at your pancreas.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve had those stones before. They took some out, but the pain came back.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, your history shows multiple ERCPs. We’ll see what the MRCP shows and talk to GI about possibly doing another procedure.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. Your MRCP was done yesterday. It shows two large stones in your pancreatic duct—one in the neck and one in the mid body.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s what’s causing the pain?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Exactly. The stone in the neck is blocking the duct, causing it to widen—now up to 10 mm. That’s worse than before. It’s likely why your pain has gotten so severe.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Can they remove them again?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ve consulted the ERCP team. They agree you need another stone extraction. They’ll schedule it as an outpatient procedure this week.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will that fix the pain?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It should help significantly. Removing the blockage will let the duct drain properly. But since you have chronic pancreatitis, you may still have some baseline pain.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my diabetes? It’s been harder to control.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, chronic pancreatitis can affect insulin production. We’re calling it secondary diabetes now. Your primary doctor will help manage it, but controlling the pancreatitis is key.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your pain is improving with Dilaudid. We’re switching you to oral hydromorphone so you can take it at home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Is that stronger than what I was on?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It’s similar to what you were taking—4 mg tablets, as needed every four hours. But don’t mix it with alcohol or drive while on it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Got it. What about my nausea meds?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re switching from prochlorperazine to promethazine. Same use—just a refill so you have it until your follow-up.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re doing well. You’ve been tolerating regular food, and your pain is much better.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yeah, I actually ate breakfast without pain.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s great progress. The GI team will call you to schedule your ERCP. In the meantime, keep taking your meds as prescribed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my other meds—amitriptyline, ziprasidone, the rest?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, resume all your home medications. We’re giving you refills on duloxetine, ziprasidone, trazodone, and the pain and nausea meds—enough to last until your PCP visit in two weeks.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: What about the eye fluttering? Should I see neurology?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Given you didn’t lose consciousness and it was brief, it’s likely not a seizure. Your history mentions pseudoseizures, possibly triggered by pain. But we’ll let your primary team decide if further evaluation is needed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good news—you’re ready to go home today. Pain is controlled, you’re eating well, and we’ve arranged your follow-up.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m glad. This pain was unbearable.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We know. The ERCP team will call you this week to schedule the stone removal. Keep taking your meds, avoid alcohol completely, and follow a low-fat diet to reduce strain on your pancreas.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve been sober for years. I won’t touch alcohol.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s excellent. Keep up the good work. Call your doctor if pain worsens or you can’t keep food down. Otherwise, see you in follow-up.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you, Doctor. I appreciate everything.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. Take care, and we’ll see how you do after the procedure.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will I need another admission for the ERCP?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: No, it’s outpatient. You’ll go in, they’ll remove the stones, and you’ll go home the same day.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That sounds better than being here again.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Agreed. Just rest, take your meds, and wait for their call.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my back pain? It’s still there, but not as bad.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We saw a small hemangioma in your L2 vertebra on the MRCP, but it’s benign and not causing issues. Your chronic back pain is separate—keep managing it as before.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, thanks for explaining everything.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Of course. You’re doing well. Let’s get your discharge papers ready.
